summary:
Para pegar (inglés):

TEPEXA (“Explore the Unknown”) is a web app that turns real NASA data into a survival and planning guide for walking on Mars. We built it on the HiRISE 1 m digital terrain model of the Margin Unit in Jezero Crater, where Perseverance collected rock samples. A student can explore scientific map layers, where every fact shows its source and certainty. An astronaut can choose science targets, set a maximum slope and an EVA time limit, and compare three routes computed on the real terrain: shortest, fastest and safest, all with the return to base. The routes use a walking-speed model, steep-slope limits and loose-soil penalties. TEPEXA then simulates the walk in 3D with the crew member and a scout drone, and produces a printable mission report with its sources, assumptions and limitations. Medusae Fossae appears as the next region, with an illustrative terrain clearly labelled as not NASA data. This matters because safe EVA planning will be key for future crewed missions, and TEPEXA makes that process visual, traceable and educational. It runs in English and Spanish, on desktop and mobile.
details:
What it does and how it works

TEPEXA is a web app for planning and rehearsing a Martian EVA (extravehicular activity) with real NASA data. It covers a 4 × 3 km area of the Margin Unit in Jezero Crater, using the HiRISE 1 m digital terrain model (USGS) and the sample sites of the Perseverance rover. It has six modules:

Martian Atlas: a 2D map with hillshade, elevation and points of interest. Every scientific fact shows its source and its certainty (confirmed, interpretation or hypothesis).

Route Planner: the user picks targets in order, a maximum slope and an EVA time limit. The server computes three routes on a 10 m grid of the real terrain (shortest, fastest and safest), always including the return to base. Walking speed follows Tobler’s hiking function calibrated to 2 km/h on flat ground, with penalties for steep slopes and loose soil.

Mission Analysis: compares the routes, shows the geology of each target, and saves the mission with a printable report that lists its sources, assumptions and limitations.

3D Simulation: the crew member walks the chosen route on the real terrain with a scout drone, with telemetry and a minimap. The map, the 3D scene and the report all use the same route geometry.

Crew and Assistant: animated team avatars, and an assistant that answers only from the mission data.

Medusae Fossae: the next region. Its walking terrain is illustrative and clearly labelled as not NASA data.

Benefits and expected impact

TEPEXA makes EVA planning visual and traceable. Students learn real Martian geology and why one path is safer than another. Mission-planning ideas can be tested before anyone walks. The same pipeline can be reused for any region that has a digital terrain model.

Tools

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, OpenLayers and Three.js (React Three Fiber).

Backend: Python with FastAPI, and PostgreSQL + PostGIS on Neon.

Hosting and quality: Render, Vercel, and GitHub Actions for automated checks.

3D models: made with Tripo and optimized with glTF-Transform (from 363 MB to 17 MB).

Hardware: no special hardware; it runs in any browser, on desktop and mobile.

Creativity

Instead of giving one “best” path, TEPEXA shows the trade-off between three. It connects a scientific map, route optimization and a 3D rehearsal through the same data, and it labels honestly what is real and what is illustrative.

Factors we considered

Safety limits: slope, EVA time and the return trip.

Data honesty: sources and certainty on every fact.

Accessibility: English and Spanish, and light 3D models so it works on phones.

Privacy: no personal data, and team avatars only with each person’s consent.

Cost: free-tier services.

Teamwork: we built it with Spec-Driven Development, using a shared API contract between backend and frontend.
